Physical design affects kinematic/dynamic complexity and closed-form solvability. Four system parts are listed. The drawing distinguishes the articulated manipulator from the distal end-effector. Viewed actual readable 1800×1013 source pixels alongside extracted text.

Programmability does not imply universal task optimality. Heavy automotive welding and fast circuit assembly motivate different compromises. Joint count, arrangement, actuation and sensing are iterative decisions. Viewed actual readable 1800×1013 source pixels alongside extracted text.

DOF is the number of independent configuration variables. Typical serial one-DOF joints are contrasted with closed-loop mobility criteria. The three-rotation drawing labels the base, middle and distal motions. The sentence calling every task mismatch redundant is overbroad. Viewed actual readable 1800×1013 source pixels alongside extracted text.

General spatial pose has three position and three orientation coordinates. Task-relative redundancy is illustrated by an axially symmetric tool whose roll can be irrelevant; reachability and actual task symmetry remain necessary qualifications. Workspace means reachable end-effector volume. Size, shape, singularities and structural/fixture interference matter. Load depends on link strength/stiffness, transmission and actuator output, configuration and dynamics. Whole-workspace guaranteed capacity must be distinguished from the allowable load at a particular configuration. Viewed actual readable 1800×1013 source pixels alongside extracted text.

Peak speed is not cycle time. Short pick-and-place moves can be acceleration/deceleration limited. Painting or welding can impose a process-limited useful travel rate. Viewed actual readable 1800×1013 source pixels alongside extracted text.

Repeatability means returning consistently to a taught point; accuracy means reaching a mathematical target. Manufacturing tolerances and kinematic calibration matter. The 0.001-inch versus 8±2-inch spray example motivates task-appropriate precision and cost. Viewed actual readable 1800×1013 source pixels alongside extracted text.

The common arm–wrist partition separates first-three-joint wrist positioning from the remaining orientation motions. Intersecting axes, zero dimensions and 0/±90-degree twists can simplify kinematics. The drawing highlights the arm and wrist portions. Cartesian positioning uses three perpendicular prismatic axes, giving a rectangular/box workspace. The side view labels vertical travel d₂ and horizontal travel d₃; the top view shows d₁. Cartesian designs combine rigidity and payload capability with linear-actuator speed limits and simple position inverse kinematics. Typical cantilevered articulated structures are less stiff but less intrusive than Cartesian structures, aiding confined access. Cost and inverse-kinematics/control comparisons are design-dependent, not universal orderings. Viewed actual readable 1800×1013 source pixels alongside extracted text.

SCARA is expanded as Selectively Compliant Assembly Robot Arm. Three parallel revolute motions and normal prismatic motion support planar assembly with height and yaw. Spherical positioning replaces the articulated elbow rotation with radial extension. The figure labels azimuth θ₁, elevation θ₂ and radial d₃, giving a shell/wedge region. Task singularity is Jacobian rank loss. det(J)=0 applies to square J. Manipulability is √det(JJᵀ), reducing to |det J| for square J. visualInspection.notes: Five outcome bullets: redundant/closed chains, actuation/transmission/selection, stiffness/compliance, position/force sensing, mobile manipulation workspace/trajectory/kinematics.

Redundancy stated as more than six DOF for full spatial pose; closed loops; distal fast precise micromanipulator DOFs; extra joints help singularity/collision avoidance. The universal 6-DOF finite-solutions and 7-DOF infinite-solutions-for-any-pose claims require reachable regular poses, rank/task/limits qualifiers. Redundancy is task-relative, not always n>6.

Closed-loop versus serial topology; Motoman L-3 joints2/3 named; increased stiffness versus generally smaller joint range/workspace. Right schematic labels moving end-effector upper platform, base below and dashed closed-loop route; three drawn struts illustrate topology, not proof of six actuators or a Motoman L-3 image.

Six linear actuators connect base and moving platform; each leg base universal joint2DOF, platform spherical joint3DOF. Fully parallel6DOF, easy inverse length computation versus complex forward pose recovery, high stiffness/load capacity and limited workspace. Right photo shows actual six-leg platform. Inverse length derived as norm(p+Rbi−ai), not printed; “often no closed-form” not a categorical impossibility.

Exact formula F=6(l−n−1)+Σ fi. l counts links including ground; n counts joints. Counts six universal2DOF, six spherical3DOF, six prismatic1DOF, n18. The formula assumes independent generic constraints; singular/special overconstrained cases need rank analysis. Photo repeats the platform, no new dimensions.

Twelve actuator links (two rigid members per telescoping actuator), one base, one platform =>l14. Sum fi12+18+6=36. F=6(14−18−1)+36=6. Continued photo no new geometry; numerical derivation is substantive incremental content.

Integrated motor, reducer and transmission design; effects on dynamic performance, control and structure. Local direct drive: actuator at/near joint output attached directly; remote drive toward base away from driven joint. Proximity alone is not sufficient to call a geared motor direct drive; use stated direct-output connection.

Spur, bevel, worm, cross-helical gears named and pictured (photos are unlabelled individually); backlash/friction; tighter mesh trades less backlash for more friction. η>1 is speed-reduction ratio, not efficiency. ωo=ωi/η and τo=ητi require ideal lossless magnitudes or consistent sign convention; actual friction acknowledged above makes unconditional exact torque equation incomplete.

Remote transmission and possible reduction; flexibility proportional to element length under unchanged material/section; tension-only requires preload or opposing active drive. Toothed belts and roller chains described as stiffer/compact, chains around smaller pulleys (qualitative comparisons need fixed design basis). Diagram small input r1 left, larger output r2 right, open belt; η=r2/r1, no slip implied, opposite ratio would be speedup.

Rotary-to-linear conversion. Left drawing direct lead-screw/nut thread contact labelled Nut; right drawing balls between threads labelled Race. Lead screws stiff/high load/high friction; ball screw recirculating bearings reduce friction and are typically backdrivable, not always self-locking. No lead/pitch equation printed; derived kinematics only if explicitly supplied.

Structural and drivetrain stiffness important. Source says most industrial robots infer tool pose via forward kinematics of sensed joint positions; do not present survey claim as timeless fact. Compliance yields sag under gravity/load and rigid-model pose error; flexibility produces resonances limiting dynamic performance/control bandwidth. Encoders alone may miss unmodelled link deformation.

Parallel k=k1+k2; series1/k=1/k1+1/k2; compliance reciprocal. For reduction stages in series, stiffness/compliance must first be referred to the same coordinate/shaft using p592; raw numbers on different shafts cannot be directly summed. Scalar linear-spring model, positive k, common generalized coordinate.

Solid round shaft torsional k=Gπd^4/(32l), d diameter not radius, l length G shear modulus. Gear output stiffness with input fixed k=Cg b r², b face width r output radius Cg material constant. Both rotational units N·m/rad, not N/m. Shaft and gear photos contain no dimensions; avoid inferring tooth counts. Formula assumes uniform linear-elastic solid shaft; hollow shaft needs polar difference not supplied.

Exact equations ko=η²ki for ideal reduction η>1; belt axial k=AE/l; hollow round cantilever end-load stiffness3πE(do^4−di^4)/(64l³); hollow square E(wo^4−wi^4)/(4l³). Belt schematic right; cantilever clamped left with downward tip-region load. Distinguish rotational transformed k from translational belt/beam k. Assumptions small linear elastic deflection, constant section, correct end-load boundary; do>di>=0, wo>wi>=0. Formulas check as3EI/l³.

Electric motors easy interface/precision; qualitative power-weight comparison with fluids; DC brushed motor stationary brushes feed rotor windings through rotating commutator. Winding overheating major limit; torque proportional current for constant flux/linear model. Generic motor cutaway at upper right does not explicitly show labelled brushes/commutator, so do not identify DC topology from photo alone.

Servo control uses desired-minus-sensed joint position error to generate force/torque command. Co-located sensor at actuator shaft is recommended. “Most effective” not a universal end-effector-accuracy guarantee; shaft sensing can miss downstream compliance p589. No sensor hardware diagram. Modern-industry prevalence claims should be source-attributed.

Strain-gauge contact force sensors: bonded to metal, output proportional strain in calibrated range. Design count/placement/stiffness/sensitivity/overload; positions actuator/wrist/fingertips; wrist3–6 wrench components. Photo shows cylindrical transducer and enlarged serpentine bonded foil gauge with two leads; do not infer total gauge count or six-axis capability from one pictured gauge. Not all possible force sensors use gauges; scope to illustrated class.

Flexure deflection creates stiffness-versus-sensitivity tradeoff; limit stops protect overload; minimizing welded/bolted joints near flexures reduces hysteresis (does not prove eliminates all hysteresis). Differential measurements improve linearity and reject shared temperature/off-axis effects under suitable arrangement, not all arbitrary differential pairs. Foil more durable/lower sensitivity; semiconductor higher sensitivity/more overload vulnerability; comparison as given.

Interdisciplinary mechanical/electrical/electronics/computer/cognitive/social sciences; autonomous mobility focus versus fixed arms; multiple competence layers; kinematics, signal analysis, information theory, AI, probability. Small four-wheel top-view schematic no dimensions or drive labels. Do not identify drive type from icon alone, or define every mobile robot as necessarily unsupervised.

Locomotion moves robot by forces against environment; source contrasts fixed-arm object manipulation. Legged locomotion uses articulated limbs and gait leg-lift/release sequence; differential/synchro/omnidirectional wheel drive names. Active COM shift may enable obstacle climbing beyond wheel size, not unconditional numerical guarantee. Drawings show biped stick figure and generic four-wheel icon, no detailed drive geometry.

Wheels efficient on flat ground and mechanically simple; general all-wheels-contact design and lower balance emphasis, not universal. Three wheels typically suffice for static stability only with noncollinear supports and COM projection inside support polygon; slope/dynamic forces can change result. Design focus traction/stability/maneuverability/control. Photo has four wheels and payload; no kinematic drive identification justified.

Wheel type plus arrangement determine wheel geometry and influence stability, maneuverability, controllability. No universally ideal configuration; choose based on environment/task constraints. Repeats some p599 ideas but adds explicit no-single-optimum application-specific tradeoff.

Workspace is attainable poses; planar chassis coordinates x,y,theta in global frame; exactly three rigid planar pose DOFs independent of internal joint count. Do not equate three configuration coordinates to three independently commandable instantaneous velocities for nonholonomic wheels. Right ellipse labelled Environment (word linebreak cosmetic), car icon and star obstacles; not all drawn region necessarily collision-free or reachable.

Arm mounted on mobile chassis extends reach; chassis gross motion versus arm fine tasks. Illustrated arm with gripper mounted on blue wheeled base; no exact DOF count justified by stylized joints/two visible wheels. Contrast of fixed-arm manipulation versus robot locomotion is illustrative, not a ban on simultaneous mobile manipulation.

Integrated actuation/transmission/sensing/stiffness/control. Adds explicit autonomy modules locomotion, perception, localization, cognition, navigation and effective mobile design base selection, stability management, configuration-space planning. Not merely excluded summary: these named topics need coverage. Mobile base plus arm expands workspace/flexibility but obstacles/limits remain.

visualInspection.notes: Title: Lecture 21, Linear Control of Manipulators, with author and institution. Actual readable 1800×1013 source pixels and extracted text were inspected; ambiguous dots/signs on pages 643,662,665 were re-rendered at 4× PDF resolution.

Learning objective is understanding the basics of linear control. Actual readable 1800×1013 source pixels and extracted text were inspected; ambiguous dots/signs on pages 643,662,665 were re-rendered at 4× PDF resolution.

Contents list feedback, second-order systems, control-law partitioning, trajectory following and disturbances. Actual readable 1800×1013 source pixels and extracted text were inspected; ambiguous dots/signs on pages 643,662,665 were re-rendered at 4× PDF resolution.

Linear differential-equation models support linear control methods. Actual manipulator dynamics are nonlinear; justified approximations can permit linear theory. Actual readable 1800×1013 source pixels and extracted text were inspected; ambiguous dots/signs on pages 643,662,665 were re-rendered at 4× PDF resolution.

Open-loop diagram: trajectory generator supplies desired position, velocity and acceleration to model-based torque computation. Torque is M(Θ_d)Θ̈_d+V(Θ_d,Θ̇_d)+G(Θ_d). No measured-output feedback branch exists. Perfect-model idealization also needs compatible initial state and no unmodeled disturbance. Stepper motors are an example of open-loop use, not universally incapable of feedback. Actual readable 1800×1013 source pixels and extracted text were inspected; ambiguous dots/signs on pages 643,662,665 were re-rendered at 4× PDF resolution.

Feedback diagram returns actual Θ and Θ̇ to the controller; trajectory generator supplies three desired signals, torque drives robot. Signals are N×1 vectors, N is joint count. Sensors measure joint position and sometimes velocity. The repeated desired-only inverse-dynamics formula is a feedforward component, not a complete feedback law. Actual readable 1800×1013 source pixels and extracted text were inspected; ambiguous dots/signs on pages 643,662,665 were re-rendered at 4× PDF resolution.

Servo error is E=Θ_d−Θ and Ė=Θ̇_d−Θ̇. A 4× PDF detail confirms the desired-velocity dot is present; OCR can miss it. Stability is explained informally as keeping errors small under moderate disturbances. Feedback must be designed for stability; its mere presence is not a guarantee. Actual readable 1800×1013 source pixels and extracted text were inspected; ambiguous dots/signs on pages 643,662,665 were re-rendered at 4× PDF resolution.

Manipulator control is coupled MIMO. Independent joint control replaces it approximately with N SISO loops. The arm photograph is illustrative and adds no numbered kinematic data. Actual readable 1800×1013 source pixels and extracted text were inspected; ambiguous dots/signs on pages 643,662,665 were re-rendered at 4× PDF resolution.

Mass–spring–damper diagram has positive x to the right and restoring/viscous forces −kx and −bẋ. The homogeneous equation is mẍ+bẋ+kx=0. m is mass, b viscous damping coefficient, k stiffness. Weak spring/heavy damping can be sluggish; stiff spring/light damping can oscillate, with formal threshold on following slides. Actual readable 1800×1013 source pixels and extracted text were inspected; ambiguous dots/signs on pages 643,662,665 were re-rendered at 4× PDF resolution.

Characteristic polynomial ms²+bs+k=0 and roots [−b±√(b²−4mk)]/(2m). Pole locations determine response. Stability classifications require the relevant physical/gain signs, not discriminant alone. Actual readable 1800×1013 source pixels and extracted text were inspected; ambiguous dots/signs on pages 643,662,665 were re-rendered at 4× PDF resolution.

Positive-parameter damping classification: discriminant positive gives real unequal overdamped poles; negative gives complex underdamped poles; zero gives critical damping. Fastest non-oscillatory language requires a fixed natural-frequency/model comparison, not arbitrary initial conditions or arbitrary design limits. The interactive link targets a local second_order_simulator_v2.html file not present in supplied files; no executable code is printed on this page. Actual readable 1800×1013 source pixels and extracted text were inspected; ambiguous dots/signs on pages 643,662,665 were re-rendered at 4× PDF resolution.

Distinct real-root solution is c₁e^(s₁t)+c₂e^(s₂t), constants from initial position and velocity. Plot shows two negative real poles, s₁ farther left than s₂. The farther-left term decays faster for stable real poles; slow-pole dominance needs a nonzero slow-mode coefficient and a sufficiently late time. Actual readable 1800×1013 source pixels and extracted text were inspected; ambiguous dots/signs on pages 643,662,665 were re-rendered at 4× PDF resolution.

Conjugate roots λ±iμ are expanded using Euler’s identity into e^(λt)[C₁cos(μt)+C₂sin(μt)]. Real motion requires the appropriate conjugate coefficients; C₁=c₁+c₂ and C₂=i(c₁−c₂). The final real constants can be written r cosδ and r sinδ. Actual readable 1800×1013 source pixels and extracted text were inspected; ambiguous dots/signs on pages 643,662,665 were re-rendered at 4× PDF resolution.

Amplitude-phase form is r e^(λt) cos(μt−δ), with r from the real cosine/sine coefficients and δ=atan2(sine coefficient,cosine coefficient). The slide reuses lowercase constants after uppercase constants on page 649; do not apply that real amplitude formula directly to the earlier complex coefficients. Pole diagram shows a left-half-plane conjugate pair and decaying oscillations; decay assumes λ<0. Actual readable 1800×1013 source pixels and extracted text were inspected; ambiguous dots/signs on pages 643,662,665 were re-rendered at 4× PDF resolution.

Normalized polynomial s²+2ζω_n s+ω_n²=0. ζ=b/(2√km), ω_n=√(k/m), λ=−ζω_n, and μ=ω_n√(1−ζ²) for the underdamped case. No damping has b=ζ=0; positive critical damping has ζ=1. Natural frequency is not damped oscillation frequency. Actual readable 1800×1013 source pixels and extracted text were inspected; ambiguous dots/signs on pages 643,662,665 were re-rendered at 4× PDF resolution.

Repeated-root solution is (c₁+c₂t)e^(−bt/(2m)); the independent t factor is essential. Plot shows coincident negative real poles and non-oscillatory decay. The polynomial-times-exponential limit uses a>0. Fastest-response wording has the same scope qualification as page 647. Actual readable 1800×1013 source pixels and extracted text were inspected; ambiguous dots/signs on pages 643,662,665 were re-rendered at 4× PDF resolution.

A right-directed actuator force f is added to the mass–spring–damper diagram, giving mẍ+bẋ+kx=f. Sensing and actuation can change the natural response. Actual readable 1800×1013 source pixels and extracted text were inspected; ambiguous dots/signs on pages 643,662,665 were re-rendered at 4× PDF resolution.

Direct zero-reference feedback is f=−k_p x−k_v ẋ. The diagram routes position through k_p and velocity through k_v to negative summing inputs. Effective coefficients become b′=b+k_v and k′=k+k_p; inertia remains m. Actual readable 1800×1013 source pixels and extracted text were inspected; ambiguous dots/signs on pages 643,662,665 were re-rendered at 4× PDF resolution.

Critical direct-feedback design uses b′=2√(mk′). Gains themselves may be negative while total effective damping/stiffness stay positive. Example m=b=k=1, desired k′=16 gives k_p=15,k_v=7 and repeated poles −4. For m>0, asymptotic stability requires both b′>0 and k′>0; equality cases need separate treatment. Actual readable 1800×1013 source pixels and extracted text were inspected; ambiguous dots/signs on pages 643,662,665 were re-rendered at 4× PDF resolution.

Control-law partitioning separates a model-based portion that simplifies the plant from a servo portion designed around the simplified model. Actual readable 1800×1013 source pixels and extracted text were inspected; ambiguous dots/signs on pages 643,662,665 were re-rendered at 4× PDF resolution.

Partitioned force f=αf′+β uses α=m and β=bẋ+kx. Exact matching cancels damping/stiffness, yielding ẍ=f′, a normalized acceleration input. Physical parameters remain in the model-based part. The actual plant is not physically stripped of mass, damping or stiffness. Actual readable 1800×1013 source pixels and extracted text were inspected; ambiguous dots/signs on pages 643,662,665 were re-rendered at 4× PDF resolution.

Servo f′=−k_v ẋ−k_p x yields ẍ+k_v ẋ+k_p x=0. Critical damping is k_v=2√k_p for k_p>0. These normalized gains have different units and values from direct force-feedback gains; parameter independence assumes exact model compensation. Actual readable 1800×1013 source pixels and extracted text were inspected; ambiguous dots/signs on pages 643,662,665 were re-rendered at 4× PDF resolution.

Partitioned diagram shows servo negative feedback, multiplication by m, and positive cancellation feedforward bẋ+kx. Example m=b=k=1,k_p=16 gives α=1,β=ẋ+x,k_v=8. Combined physical force equals −15x−7ẋ, matching the earlier direct design. Actual readable 1800×1013 source pixels and extracted text were inspected; ambiguous dots/signs on pages 643,662,665 were re-rendered at 4× PDF resolution.

Trajectory following needs smooth desired x_d, ẋ_d and ẍ_d. Error e=x_d−x; servo acceleration f′=ẍ_d+k_v ė+k_p e. The feedback acts in error coordinates and includes desired acceleration feedforward. Actual readable 1800×1013 source pixels and extracted text were inspected; ambiguous dots/signs on pages 643,662,665 were re-rendered at 4× PDF resolution.

Substitution yields ë+k_v ė+k_p e=0 under exact unit-mass model. Diagram has desired-minus-actual comparators, positive error gains and acceleration feedforward, then model-based scaling/cancellation. Any response wording means choosing this ideal second-order polynomial, not arbitrary realizable hardware performance. Actual readable 1800×1013 source pixels and extracted text were inspected; ambiguous dots/signs on pages 643,662,665 were re-rendered at 4× PDF resolution.

Forced error model is printed ë+k_v ė+k_p e=f_dist. A high-resolution detail confirms the physical disturbance arrow enters a MINUS summing input after the mass gain. Thus a resisting physical force F_dist gives normalized error forcing F_dist/m; the reused symbol needs an explicit mass/unit convention. This is a forced second-order error model. Actual readable 1800×1013 source pixels and extracted text were inspected; ambiguous dots/signs on pages 643,662,665 were re-rendered at 4× PDF resolution.

BIBO means bounded disturbance magnitude implies bounded error for a stable closed-loop transfer function. Printed max f_dist<a omits absolute value; an upper bound alone does not bound negative excursions. Closed-loop stability must be assumed, and bounded does not mean zero error. Actual readable 1800×1013 source pixels and extracted text were inspected; ambiguous dots/signs on pages 643,662,665 were re-rendered at 4× PDF resolution.

For constant normalized error forcing d and stable positive k_p,k_v, steady-state derivatives vanish and e_ss=d/k_p. Larger positive k_p reduces magnitude for a fixed nonzero d. Error is never zero requires nonzero disturbance and finite gain; it is not true for zero forcing. Actual readable 1800×1013 source pixels and extracted text were inspected; ambiguous dots/signs on pages 643,662,665 were re-rendered at 4× PDF resolution.

Integral action adds k_i∫e dt to servo and error equation. High-resolution rendering confirms the differentiated equation has e triple-dot and f_dist DOT on the right. Constant forcing has zero derivative after its onset. Stable steady state with k_i≠0 can yield e=0. The characteristic polynomial is s³+k_v s²+k_p s+k_i; positive gains alone do not guarantee stability. Initial integrator state and onset discontinuities must not be erased by differentiation. Actual readable 1800×1013 source pixels and extracted text were inspected; ambiguous dots/signs on pages 643,662,665 were re-rendered at 4× PDF resolution.

visualInspection.notes: Supervised trees support classification and regression; hierarchical sequential tests partition data until pure or another stop. Animal tree: feathers true leads can-fly true hawk / false penguin; feathers false leads has-fins true dolphin / false bear. Four leaves, three tests, two edges on each root-leaf path. The visible optional mglearn plot_animal_tree call is not itself model training. No claim that these four classes exhaust all animals. Actual 1800-pixel rendering and footer inspected.

Root receives the training subset for this tree; branches encode test outcomes; internal nodes test data. The diagram shows root, two children and a deeper right branch. A tree that does not split may have a root that is itself a leaf; do not universalize the illustrated first split. Actual 1800-pixel rendering and footer inspected.

Continuous feature test x_j>omega_m creates an axis-parallel binary split. Equality at the threshold goes to the false branch. Categorical equality example color==red is binary despite the adjacent claim of an n-way split; a separate branch for each category is a different multiway test, not a consequence of equality alone. Preserve that qualification. Actual 1800-pixel rendering and footer inspected.

Univariate tests use one feature; multivariate linear tests sum w_j*x_j+b and can create oblique hyperplanes. A univariate tree can use different features at different nodes. Most-informative refers to the chosen local impurity or MSE criterion, not proof of a globally optimal full tree. Classification impurity differs from regression squared-error objective. Actual 1800-pixel rendering and footer inspected.

Diagram has four decision nodes including root, five leaves, nine total nodes, eight edges and maximum root-to-leaf depth three edges. Leaf means no further split, not necessarily all leaves at same depth or pure. Classification predicts the leaf majority class; squared-error regression predicts mean target, not mean input vector. Actual 1800-pixel rendering and footer inspected.

Visible partition uses horizontal y=2.5, then lower-region x=4.5. Lower-left leaf has four blue points and is pure; upper region has four red and two blue points, so is mixed despite red majority fill; lower-right has one red. Axis-parallel numeric paths define hyperrectangles, possibly unbounded; linear oblique tests give polyhedral intersections. Maximum depth, minimum sample count or insufficient impurity decrease can stop before purity. Pure training leaves can overfit. Actual 1800-pixel rendering and footer inspected.

Table contrasts discrete-label classification with continuous-target regression, majority versus mean leaf prediction and impurity versus within-branch squared error. The mean statement is for the displayed squared-error regression setup, not all possible loss functions. Both use recursive partitioning; feature type alone does not decide task type. Actual 1800-pixel rendering and footer inspected.

Synthetic humanoid fall classification: inputs Acc_Z vertical acceleration and Gyro_X named pitch rate by this source; targets 0 stable, 1 forward, 2 backward. Preserve source axis naming rather than claim universal sensor-frame convention. Small trees provide visible if/else paths, but no universal faster-than-all-NN/SVM or real-world fall-safety claim follows. Actual 1800-pixel rendering and footer inspected.

Actual imports: NumPy, pyplot, DecisionTreeClassifier and plot_tree from sklearn.tree, DecisionBoundaryDisplay from sklearn.inspection, train_test_split, ListedColormap. Distinct estimation, tree visualization, feature-plane visualization, split and palette roles. ListedColormap accepts supported color specifications, not only hexadecimal codes. Actual 1800-pixel rendering and footer inspected.

Actual code fixes np.random.seed(42), N=150 per class; stable normal means [9.8,0] scales [0.5,10], forward [4,150] scales [2,30], backward [4,-150] scales [2,30], all size (N,2). Normal scale arguments are standard deviations, not variances. vstack gives X (450,2); labels [0]*N+[1]*N+[2]*N give y (450,), aligned class blocks. Synthetic independent Gaussian draws are illustrative and unbounded, not measured robot guarantees. Actual 1800-pixel rendering and footer inspected.

Flowchart splits one dataset into training and test subsets and sends training data into the decision tree. A final prediction alone is not validation; held-out labels are needed for score. Diagram does not explicitly draw a test-to-score connector, so preserve shown architecture without inventing deployment validation. Actual 1800-pixel rendering and footer inspected.

Pre-pruning limits growth; post-pruning evaluates replacing subtrees using a pruning/validation criterion. Actual named controls max_depth, min_samples_leaf and max_leaf_nodes. Source inaccurately describes min_samples_leaf as a parent split-count condition and says scikit-learn has no post-pruning; current official documentation and installed version support ccp_alpha cost-complexity pruning. Preserve this version-specific correction and distinguish min_samples_split from child-leaf minimum. Actual 1800-pixel rendering and footer inspected.

Actual train_test_split uses test_size=0.3, stratify=y, random_state=42; 450 total yields 315 train and 135 test, balanced 105/45 per class. DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=3, random_state=42) is pre-pruned, then fit(X_tr,y_tr). max_depth is a maximum edge depth from root zero, not exactly three levels or a guarantee the fit reaches that depth. Actual 1800-pixel rendering and footer inspected.

Feature-plane output has x acceleration, y Gyro_X tilt rate; blue stable cluster near x9.8,y0, red forward high positive rate and green backward negative rate. Horizontal predicted bands reflect this fitted tree using Gyro_X splits, not a universal inability to use Acc_Z. Plotted color names differ from automatic node colors on next page, so classes follow labels not cross-figure color assumptions. Actual 1800-pixel rendering and footer inspected.

Actual tree: root Gyro_X<=-45.452 with315 samples, value[105,105,105], printed class Stable; true leaf backward [0,0,105]. False child Gyro_X<=61.097 has210 samples [105,105,0]; true stable [105,0,0], false forward [0,105,0]. Root and right child are ties, not strict majority despite source wording. Printed thresholds are rounded; use exact displayed-rule hypothetical for equality questions, not claim bit-exact estimator thresholds. Tree has two decision nodes, three leaves, depth2, although maximum allowed3. Actual 1800-pixel rendering and footer inspected.

Tree strengths: visible simple rules and no usual need for feature standardization in ideal axis-aligned comparisons. Complete scaling invariance needs qualification for finite precision and transforms that change ordering. Ordinary constant-leaf regression can evaluate out-of-range inputs but does not extend a trend; prediction remains a leaf target summary rather than necessarily the last chronological target. High variance under small training changes can persist despite pruning; not a universal failure claim. Actual 1800-pixel rendering and footer inspected.

Forest ensembles combine randomized trees to reduce variance/overfitting under suitable diversity; averaging identical perfectly correlated predictions does not create the benefit. Randomization encourages diversity, not a mathematical guarantee every tree is unique or every dataset accuracy improves. Actual 1800-pixel rendering and footer inspected.

Bootstrap draws n rows with replacement from n original rows, retaining n draws but possibly fewer distinct observations. Examples [2,5,3,2,5] omit1,4; [3,1,1,4,3] omit2,5. Approximate omitted fraction is an expectation near e^-1 for large n, not an exact one-third in each sample. Derived finite-n nonselection probability (1-1/n)^n is explicitly a mathematical extension of the stated sampling process. Actual 1800-pixel rendering and footer inspected.

Random feature selection occurs at each node, not once as one fixed subset for the whole tree; max_features controls the candidate feature count and the best split is selected within that subset, rather than necessarily choosing a random threshold. Actual 1800-pixel rendering and footer inspected.

Regression averages numerical tree outputs; classification averages the per-tree class probabilities before choosing the largest mean probability, which is not necessarily the majority of hard tree labels. Randomized construction encourages, but does not guarantee, different trees. Actual 1800-pixel rendering and footer inspected.

The flowchart separates training from test data, draws bootstrap training subsets, fits separate trees, and aggregates their predictions; it does not train trees sequentially on residuals as boosting would. Actual 1800-pixel rendering and footer inspected.

The example imports RandomForestClassifier and constructs n_estimators=5, random_state=2 before fit(X_train,y_train); these data variable names are not defined by the snippet and differ from earlier X_tr. Five means trees, not features or classes. The classifier default max_features is sqrt, not a universal regressor default. Actual 1800-pixel rendering and footer inspected.

Five individual-tree panels and a combined ensemble show two labeled classes, blue circles and red triangles, unlike the earlier three-class synthetic fall data. Exact input coordinates are unavailable; these pictures must not be claimed as reproduced from the earlier 450-row robot example. Their axis-aligned boundaries differ and combine without proving universal smoothing or accuracy. Actual 1800-pixel rendering and footer inspected.

Increasing n_estimators generally adds cost and may stabilize averaging, but does not guarantee monotonically better test accuracy. Setting max_features to every feature removes feature subsampling, not bootstrap randomness. The printed regression default log2(n_features) conflicts with the official RandomForestRegressor current default 1.0, meaning all features. The classifier sqrt default is distinct. Nearly always better is not demonstrated by a benchmark here. Actual 1800-pixel rendering and footer inspected.

Axis-aligned forests usually do not need feature standardization, which does not eliminate other preprocessing needs. Trees can be built independently and n_jobs controls parallel jobs, not the number of trees. Memory/time comparisons and high-dimensional limitations depend on the problem. A regression forest can output predictions outside the observed input range; averaging leaf means does not extend a learned numerical trend beyond the training target range, and need not return the last chronological sample. Actual 1800-pixel rendering and footer inspected.

Summary lists tree tests, pruning, bootstrap and feature randomization, plus applications to terrain, fault diagnosis, UAV navigation and defect inspection. The universal statement that forests outperform a single tree on all robotics benchmarks is unsupported by evidence on this slide. Prototype-versus-production advice is a heuristic, not a mandatory or safety-validated deployment rule. Actual 1800-pixel rendering and footer inspected.

Reference-only slide listing Müller and Guido, Alpaydin and official scikit-learn tree and RandomForestClassifier documentation; no new examinable proposition. Actual 1800-pixel rendering and footer inspected.

Recap contrasts labeled supervised mapping and unlabeled unsupervised regularities; RL uses interaction and evaluative feedback rather than correct-action labels. Third branch is a pedagogical taxonomy, not an exhaustive universal classification. Actual readable 1800×1013 source pixels inspected alongside text.

Teacher-versus-critic table: prescribed labeled guidance versus evaluation, often scarce/delayed feedback and learned intermediate values. Feedback need not always be delayed or sparse; later dense rewards are compatible. Actual readable 1800×1013 source pixels inspected alongside text.

Trial-and-error example and complete loop diagram: actions travel agent to environment; observations, next state s_(t+1) and reward r_(t+1) return. Dog/treat is analogy, not a required formal action-label dataset. Actual readable 1800×1013 source pixels inspected alongside text.
Agent is learner/decision-maker; environment is outside the modeled agent. Mobile robot/maze example. Boundary is a modeling choice. Actual readable 1800×1013 source pixels inspected alongside text.

Action a_t belongs to action set A; four maze directions are discrete, steering angle can be continuous. Arrows lead from agent to environment. Actual readable 1800×1013 source pixels inspected alongside text.

Return arrow carries observations/state information and numerical reward. State is complete situation description; observation can be partial, as next page explicitly names o_t separately. Actual readable 1800×1013 source pixels inspected alongside text.

Loop uses o_t of s_t to choose a_t, yielding s_(t+1), new observation and r_(t+1). Episode/trial runs from start to terminal in the pedagogical episodic setting. Later continuing task is practically truncated. Actual readable 1800×1013 source pixels inspected alongside text.

Deterministic policy pi:S→A; stochastic pi(a|s) action distribution. Sarsa on-policy and Q-learning off-policy. Regardless of exploration strategy is too broad without sufficient data coverage/convergence conditions. Actual readable 1800×1013 source pixels inspected alongside text.

Finite undiscounted return sums T rewards from r_(t+1). Infinite discounted return uses powers gamma^(i−1), with 0≤gamma<1. Gamma=0 is immediate-only; closer to one retains distant weights. Bounded rewards plus discount give convergence; time limit is not the only reason for discounting. Actual readable 1800×1013 source pixels inspected alongside text.

Optimal value max over policies; Q*(s,a) fixes first action then optimal continuation; V*(s)=max_a Q*(s,a). Expected return, not guaranteed realization; optimal actions can tie. Actual readable 1800×1013 source pixels inspected alongside text.

Bellman derivation splits first reward from discounted tail; next-state transition distribution P(s_next|s,a). Expectations should be conditioned on current state/action and optimal continuation, omitted in compact notation. Actual readable 1800×1013 source pixels inspected alongside text.

State/action Bellman forms and bracket labels inspected. Q*=expected immediate reward plus gamma-weighted expectation of max next Q; V* maximizes current action. Greedy optimal policy needs actual Q*, not arbitrary current estimates. Actual readable 1800×1013 source pixels inspected alongside text.

Exploration gathers information; exploitation follows best current estimate. Source calls exploitation highest immediate reward, but Q values encode cumulative return. Excessive exploit can miss better actions; excessive explore sacrifices use of learned behavior, not a universal theorem of failure. Actual readable 1800×1013 source pixels inspected alongside text.

Model-free examples Q-learning/Sarsa versus fully known model dynamic programming with value/policy iteration. Model-based does not generally require perfect prior knowledge or eliminate all exploration; learned models exist. Model-free does not mean no learned Q model. Actual readable 1800×1013 source pixels inspected alongside text.

Q update with eta learning rate, gamma discount, sampled reward plus max estimated next value minus old estimate. Last Q omits hat typographically. Future value remains estimated, not wholly observed; convergence claim needs finite/tabular and sampling/step-size assumptions. Actual readable 1800×1013 source pixels inspected alongside text.

Full pseudocode initializes Q outside episodes, initializes s per episode, epsilon-greedy chooses a, observes r and s_next, updates Q, assigns s=s_next and repeats until terminal. Side box gives exploration-branch epsilon and exploitation-branch 1−epsilon. Random exploration can also select greedy action; terminal bootstrap convention omitted. Actual readable 1800×1013 source pixels inspected alongside text.

Diagram receives current gripper location and target 3D location; Q-learning reaches target, then separate gripper closing is shown. Reachability and grasping success are not guaranteed; subsequent FetchReach code is not a grasping task. Actual readable 1800×1013 source pixels inspected alongside text.

Gymnasium standard environment API: make, reset, step, render; environments and wrappers support comparable experiments. It is not itself the MuJoCo physics engine or a complete RL training algorithm. Actual readable 1800×1013 source pixels inspected alongside text.

MuJoCo models dynamics/contact/gravity for simulation before hardware. Four illustrations: pick/place, navigation, humanoid, object manipulation. Sim-to-real support is not a guarantee of safe or successful transfer. Actual readable 1800×1013 source pixels inspected alongside text.

Notebook shell command !pip install gymnasium-robotics mujoco matplotlib -q. FetchReachDense-v4: 7-DOF robot, 4-component continuous input, dense reward minus Euclidean goal error. Reward is nonpositive, not strictly negative at zero distance. The environment blocks the gripper channel; do not infer grasping. Actual readable 1800×1013 source pixels inspected alongside text.

Imports gymnasium as gym, gymnasium_robotics, numpy as np and pyplot; gym.register_envs(gymnasium_robotics), env=gym.make("FetchReachDense-v4"). Dense means per-step distance reward. Registration does not instantiate every robot model; current compatibility helper may be no-op after import. Actual readable 1800×1013 source pixels inspected alongside text.

NX=NY=NZ=8; BIN_SIZE=0.04; N_ACTIONS=6. Float32 ACTION_MAP rows [+x,−x,+y,−y,+z,−z], fourth component zero. Unit normalized commands are not guaranteed one metre or exactly one bin of achieved motion. Underlying API remains continuous while agent chooses six vectors. Actual readable 1800×1013 source pixels inspected alongside text.

Q=zeros((NX,NY,NZ,N_ACTIONS)); alpha=.1,gamma=.95,epsilon=.5. get_state: err=desired_goal−achieved_goal; tuple(clip(((err+.16)/BIN_SIZE).astype(int),0,7)). visualInspection.notes: Six illustrated cards: perception identifies scene objects/people/obstacles/layout; localization estimates position and orientation from landmarks/odometry; manipulation uses visual feedback and force sensing; interaction recognizes gestures/expressions/intent; navigation plans collision-free paths in dynamic scenes; inspection detects defects/anomalies/wear. Do not conflate localization with path planning.

Vision described as inverse of graphics: 2D observations infer 3D world properties, whereas graphics renders 3D models. Desired properties shape, illumination and color distributions. Inverse does not imply unique reconstruction.

Camera-eye, algorithm-brain analogy. Figure camera sensor with lens and CCD/CMOS → processing with image processing, feature extraction and ML models → recognition, navigation/obstacle avoidance and manipulation. Read all box text and directed arrows.

Projection loses depth; apparent size alone cannot distinguish size/distance. Figure contrasts human object labels Chair/Dog/Tree/Table with robot Feature extraction/Edge detection/Uncertainty and Object?; schematic is not a theorem that machines cannot recognize objects.

Diagram adds extracted-text-missing history: 1970s early scene understanding includes line labeling (3D from 2D line drawings), pictorial structures (flexible parts), Marr’s Paradigm with Computational Theory (Goal), Algorithm (Method), then a repeated Marr’s Paradigm bullet instead of a distinct third level. 1980s: pyramids/scale-space multi-resolution, regularization smoothness for ill-posed problems, MRF probabilistic global optimization. 1990s–Present: SfM reconstruction, computational photography HDR/panoramas/texture synthesis, deep learning. Preserve timeline as source attribution; do not silently repair incomplete Marr list.

Eight named mappings: OCR documents/packages; mechanical inspection tolerances/defects; medical CT/MRI analysis; autonomous vehicles/drones and SLAM; image stitching panoramas; AR tracked reference points with virtual models in live feed; biometrics face/fingerprint authentication; visual effects morphing/stabilization.

E(lambda) spectral intensity; medium absorption changes spectrum; slide attributes white-light dispersion to Newton in1670. Approximate visible range400–700nm. Plot normalized intensity versus wavelength300–1000nm: orange Sun5778K peaks around500nm; blue Lamp2600K rises across plotted interval, reaching its displayed maximum at1000nm. Independent normalization means no absolute emitted-power inference. Rainbow400–750nm. Do not infer lamp true peak is1000nm from plot boundary.

Printed L(lambda)=E(lambda)R(lambda) W m^-2, R in[0,1], diagram illuminant→surface reflectance→eye spectral response M(lambda). Simplified spectral product omits geometric radiometry and spectral-density units; use declared relative/discrete-band conventions in numerical examples. Rods more sensitive, intensity/night; cones daylight/color. Response integrates product of received spectrum and sensitivity.

Trichromatic compression into rho,gamma,beta with integrals L(lambda) times Mr,Mg,Mb. Upper normalized L/M/S curves overlap, peaks approximately570/545/445nm; L responds at medium as well as long wavelengths, not pure red-only channels. Lower plot shows three colored weighted spectral areas but no numbers defining exact integrals. Distinguish three responses from full spectrum.

Tristimulus value is3-vector rho,gamma,beta. Red-brick weighted spectral areas repeat lower plot from932; integrates areas, not just peak heights. Dominant L-cone response in this illustrated example, not an illumination-independent universal property of every red material.

Exact arrow pipeline: Real World → Optics (Lens/Aperture/shutter) → Sensor CCD/CMOS → Gain ISO → ADC → ISP Demosaic down to Denoise right to White balance up to Gamma right to Compress → RGB Image. Sensor chip encloses sensor/gain/ADC; photosites silicon regular array analogous to cones/retina. Ordering is the shown simplified pipeline, not a universal ISP sequence; sharpening/color correction added in later prose but not in diagram.

Actual figure contrasts CCD photon-to-electron in array, shifted charge to common charge-voltage conversion/output amplifier, versus CMOS pixel-local conversion and addressing. Prose CCD Charge-Coupled Device correct; CMOS expansion printed Complementary Metal Oxide on Silicon differs from standard semiconductor wording and must not be silently accepted. Simplified per-pixel amplifier description is a readout contrast, not proof of every commercial layout.

Color filter array above gray silicon photosites; colored Bayer grid has 2green/1red/1blue per2x2 tile, filters overlap spectrally. Gain ISO amplifies sensed signal before ADC; ADC converts analog voltage to discrete value. Gain does not collect extra incident photons; source exposure wording is simplified.

Demosaicing estimates two missing color values per CFA pixel via neighbors, producing three color planes. Shot noise identified as photon-count variance, dark current as thermal electrons. Denoising reduces graininess especially low light. Sharpening edge enhancement compensates lens/demosaic blur; cannot assume perfect detail recovery.

White balance channel gains aim for neutral equal RGB under illuminant changes. Color correction uses3x3 or3x4 C mapping camera responses toward CIE XYZ/sRGB because camera filters do not perfectly match cones. This color matrix C is not the later geometric3x4 camera projection matrix C. Gamma power-law encoding approximates perceptual/display response and is distinct from final JPEG compression; no exact gamma exponent or universal log law specified.

Actual diagram: light source illuminates a surface with normal n-hat; scattered rays include green ray through optics O to rear sensor plane. A separate virtual image plane is in front. Image formation maps 3D to 2D with depth loss; do not confuse physical rear sensor with front virtual plane.

Upright object left, small aperture middle, inverted smaller real image right. Ideal pinhole requires no focusing adjustment but transmits little light. Do not extend ideal ray model to unlimited sharpness or ignore diffraction when making physical claims.

Thin convex lens collects more light; diagram real upright object left and inverted real image right with focal points and equivalent pinhole. Printed 1/|zo|+1/|zi|=1/f applies to illustrated real-object/real-image distances; virtual-image calculations need an explicitly supplied sign convention. Simplified eye single crystalline lens and camera compound glass/plastic lenses comparison does not establish that cornea has no optical role.

Virtual image plane f in front of camera center C gives non-inverted x=fX/Z and y=fY/Z. Camera axes and principal point shown. Require Z nonzero, and Z positive for visible front points under supplied convention. Homogeneous map is linear before division, ordinary perspective projection is nonlinear. Scale of a 3D point along a viewing ray is lost.

Homogeneous metric p=(fX,fY,Z), dehomogenized x=p1/p3, y=p2/p3. Homogeneous camera point (X,Y,Z,1); Cmetric=[[f,0,0,0],[0,f,0,0],[0,0,1,0]]. World point transformed into camera frame by inverse camera pose: CP=(OTC)^-1 OP. Actual diagram separates world O and camera C frames and point rays. Homogeneous scales and mixed units must be explained in calculations.

Sensor W by H pixels, photosite physical side lengths w and h. Upper-left pixel origin(0,0), u right and v down, last indices W-1/H-1. Principal point is optical-axis intersection, not necessarily pixel origin or exact sensor center. Positive x/y directions in virtual plane align with u/v in shown convention.

Principal point(u0,v0) is optical-axis intersection; u=x/w+u0, v=y/h+v0. Homogeneous matrix[[1/w,0,u0],[0,1/h,v0],[0,0,1]] acts on metric homogeneous image; output third coordinate printed w-tilde is projective scale, not photosite width w. Figure repeats top-left origin and axes; empty lower-right outlined box contains no evidence.

K=[[f/w,0,u0],[0,f/h,v0],[0,0,1]], Q=[I3|0], C=KQ(OTC)^-1. Intrinsics versus world-to-camera extrinsics. Formula labels pixel homogeneous vector with metric-looking x/y/z tildes; distinguish by declared coordinates. Printed final-pixel rounding is an indexing convention, not a requirement to discard subpixel coordinates in all vision algorithms. Rigid pose inverse is crucial.

Six recap bullets repeat inverse vision, eye/brain, depth loss, optics/electronics, pinhole/lens and camera intrinsic/extrinsic matrix. P label1,N label0; explicit linear-separability assumption; seek weights w0..wn; correct classification leaves parameters unchanged. The next page main prose discusses positive errors, but its actual pseudocode inset includes both positive and negative updates. Convergence depends on the full algorithm and stated separability.

Actual pseudocode inset contains BOTH updates: positive example with w·x<0 adds x; negative example with w·x>=0 subtracts x. Thus equality is correctly positive. Inset explicitly samples P union N until convergence. Main prose discusses only positive errors, and falsely suggests one addition yields a positive dot product. It increases the dot product by ||x||² but may remain negative; adding x also need not increase every weight component. Angle formula needs nonzero vectors. Treat bias consistently through explicit augmented input.

Step function is already nonlinear: y1 for z>=0,0 otherwise. The claimed need to introduce nonlinearity should instead distinguish differentiability/useful gradients for ordinary backpropagation. Tanh formula and curve pass through(0,0), saturate toward±1; sigmoid formula/curve pass through(0,0.5), approach0 and1. Both formula plots visually confirmed.

Table prints closed sigmoid[0,1] and tanh[-1,1] ranges although finite real inputs attain open ranges; endpoints are limits. Tanh is zero-centered, not universally preferred. Both may saturate. Products of small gradients can attenuate early-layer signal. Printed shared example max derivative0.25 is sigmoid-specific: tanh maximum is1. Loss compares predicted output to actual labels, common cross-entropy for classification and MSE regression. Printed used during training only is false if labelled validation/test loss is computed without updates; ordinary unlabelled inference need not compute supervised loss.

Training adjusts weights/biases to minimize loss. Lists gradient calculation, backward error propagation, gradient descent opposite gradient. Distinguish chain-rule gradient computation (backprop) from chosen optimizer update; neither alone implies global minimum.

Historical list: dead reckoning uses speed, direction, and time; resection intersects landmark bearings; celestial navigation uses star elevations and tables; Harrison’s chronometer supports longitude; GPS is associated with a 1995 milestone and indoor/urban obstruction; probabilistic methods include Bayes and Kalman filtering, with 1960 named. The resection diagram shows bearing intersections. Dates are retained as source wording, not independent chronology research. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside extracted text.

Five uncertainty categories: changing environment; noisy or limited sensors; actuator noise and wear; approximate models; algorithmic tradeoffs. The comparison with deterministic industrial robots is an idealization, not an absence of physical uncertainty. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside extracted text.

Perception turns raw sensor measurements into a useful description of the environment. This repeats the p1373 definition and is linked without padding. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside extracted text.

Five-stage pipeline: acquisition, filtering, segmentation, feature extraction, interpretation. The example starts with 360 ranges, discards four zero-valued bad returns, and retains 356. A gap greater than 20 cm splits three clusters. Line fits produce three wall segments; two long parallel walls and one short wall are interpreted as a corridor. That interpretation is illustrative, not a uniqueness proof. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside extracted text.

Pulsed LiDAR time of flight: d = ct/2, c = 3 × 10^8 m/s, round-trip time 40 ns, distance 6 m. Each orange point is a range-angle measurement. Approximate RPLidar values are 5.5 Hz, 360 points per revolution, and 12 m maximum range; no model is named. These are illustrative, not universal product specifications. Some RPLIDAR models use triangulation rather than direct pulsed time of flight. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside extracted text.

Encoder example: wheel radius 0.05 m, circumference about 0.314 m, 1000 pulses per revolution, about 0.314 mm per pulse, and 620 pulses giving about 0.195 m. Travel assumes calibration and no slip. A gyro reading 30 degrees per second for 2 seconds gives a 60-degree change, not absolute heading without an initial reference. Accelerometer gravity-based tilt interpretation needs a near-static or dynamic-acceleration qualification. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside extracted text.

Ten wall ranges: 1.98, 2.03, 2.01, 1.97, 2.02, 2.00, 1.99, 2.04, 1.96, 2.01 m. Mean is 2.001 m and population-convention standard deviation is about 0.02468 m. The slide rounds these to 2.00 m and 0.025 m. Distinguish population and sample conventions, standard deviation and hard bounds, and Gaussian mean from a true value unless unbiasedness is assumed. Actual printed footer is 9, not physical-offset value 11. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside extracted text.

Position tracking starts from an approximately known pose. Global localization starts with a known map but an unknown initial pose. The target illustration is decorative, not a calibrated uncertainty plot. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside extracted text.

Belief is a conditional probability distribution over planar pose (x, y, θ), recursively informed by control and noisy observations. The two-dimensional Gaussian position plot labels sigma 20. Its negative vertical baseline supports projected contours and does not represent negative probability. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside extracted text.

State may include pose, velocity, objects, and landmarks. Transition and measurement models are distinct. Graph arrows are x_(t−1) to x_t, u_t to x_t, and x_t to z_t. The posterior conditions on all available histories; the bottom predicted belief omits z_t despite reusing unbarred bel typography. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside extracted text.

A complete state screens off earlier history conditional on the relevant state and control. Both conditional-independence equations were inspected. Current or future controls are not made irrelevant by the Markov assumption. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside extracted text.

Bayes prediction integrates the motion model against the previous belief; correction multiplies by likelihood and normalizes. The no-assumption claim cannot mean absence of motion, measurement, or Markov assumptions. It is qualified as freedom from a fixed linear/Gaussian family. Zero total evidence cannot be normalized directly. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside extracted text.

Multivariate Gaussian density has an inverse and determinant normalization. Mean and symmetric covariance are shown, including all pose variances and cross-covariances. Covariance is a central second moment and is positive semidefinite; the ordinary full-dimensional density requires positive definiteness. Singular cases need separate support treatment. A single Gaussian is unimodal; a mixture is a different representation. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside extracted text.

Particles are candidate states approximating a possibly multimodal, non-Gaussian belief. The graph places sample marks beneath a skewed curve. A blanket threshold of 100 or more particles is not a universal accuracy certificate. Finite-sample error, bias, complexity, and sampling quality are distinct; more particles cost more computation without guaranteeing lower error on every realization. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside extracted text.

Linear transition x_t = F_t x_(t−1) + G_t u_t + v_t and measurement z_t = H_t x_t + w_t use zero-mean Gaussian noises with covariances V_t and W_t. The initial belief is Gaussian. The LTI introductory wording is narrower than known time-varying linear filtering. Exact Gaussian posterior and optimality statements require the usual noise-independence and correct-model assumptions. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside extracted text.

All Kalman equations inspected: mean Fμ + Gu; covariance FPFᵀ + V; gain P̄Hᵀ(HP̄Hᵀ + W)⁻¹; mean plus gain times innovation; covariance (I − KH)P̄. The innovation inverse requires nonsingularity. Optimality is conditional on the model and noise assumptions. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside extracted text.

Scalar prediction: initial mean 2, variance 0.25, control 2, process variance 0.5, and F = G = 1 give mean 4 and variance 0.75. The blue prior is centered at 2 and narrower; the dashed red prediction is centered at 4 and wider. Variance is not standard deviation. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside extracted text.

Measurement 5 with variance 0.3 and H = 1 gives gain 5/7, posterior mean 33/7, and variance 3/14. The cyan measurement peak is at 5; the solid red posterior lies between prediction and measurement and is narrower. The source’s under-reporting slip is a specified example, not a universal slip-bias direction. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside extracted text.

First-order EKF Taylor expansions were inspected. Motion Jacobians use the previous corrected state and zero noise; measurement Jacobians use the predicted state and zero noise. The printed motion evaluation x_t = μ_(t−1) has a time-index mismatch with differentiation with respect to x_(t−1). Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside extracted text.

EKF covariance uses F_x P F_xᵀ + F_v V F_vᵀ. Innovation covariance uses H_x P̄ H_xᵀ + H_w W H_wᵀ. The mean is propagated by nonlinear f, not just a Jacobian product. This is a local approximation, not exact arbitrary nonlinear Gaussian inference. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside extracted text.

The odometry transform is T_new = T_old Trans_x(d) Rot(Δθ). Translation is along the old heading before rotation. Since the product includes the old world pose, the result is the new world pose rather than only a relative increment. The distance and orientation diagram was inspected. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside extracted text.

The noisy motion uses distance noise v_d and heading noise v_θ. F_x = [[1,0,−d sinθ],[0,1,d cosθ],[0,0,1]] and F_v = [[cosθ,0],[sinθ,0],[0,1]]. Both full matrices were inspected. The old-heading translation model is not exact finite circular-arc integration during simultaneous forward motion and turning. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside extracted text.

Differential-drive diagram: d is half the track width; φ is world heading. Forward speed is (v_r + v_l)/2; heading rate is (v_r − v_l)/(2d). Wheel tangential speeds are radius times angular rates. World velocities are v cosφ and v sinφ. All diagram labels and equations were inspected. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside extracted text.

The full Python raster snippet was transcribed. Vt is defined from distance and converted angular standard deviations, but EKF(robot=(robot,V)) refers to undefined V in a clean namespace. RandomPath supplies control. E0 is an initial covariance. The code runs numerical and animation stages, invokes HTML without supplied notebook imports, and plots blue truth, red estimate, and green ellipses. The angular input is 0.5 degrees in code although prose omits units. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside extracted text.

Odometry-only plots show separated blue ground truth and red estimate, with green positional uncertainty ellipses. The prose calls q a method; the pinned toolbox defines it as a state property. A confidence level cannot be inferred from the ellipse appearance alone. Accumulating motion uncertainty does not mean every covariance entry grows monotonically. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside extracted text.

Known global landmark coordinates and unknown robot pose define localization. Range is Euclidean distance and bearing is relative to robot heading, with additive range/bearing noise. The printed single-argument arctangent loses quadrant information and fails when its denominator is zero; the explicit correction is atan2 with wrapping. Coincident robot and landmark positions make bearing and the regular Jacobian undefined. Landmark extraction is the example’s representation choice, not mandatory for every localization system. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside extracted text.

Pinned RTB expands workspace to [−10,10] on each axis, unlike the 10×10 prose. P0 is covariance, not pose. The animate alias runs with a deprecation warning in RTB 1.4.4. A measurement and landmark ID select the appropriate known map coordinate for correction. The printed H_x has three sign errors for differentiation with respect to robot pose. The correct local matrix is [[−Δx/r,−Δy/r,0],[Δy/r²,−Δx/r²,−1]] and H_w is identity. Gain, innovation, and covariance equations were inspected. The map and trajectory overlay illustrate localization and correction, not zero-error proof. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside extracted text.

Timeline figure: FFT algorithms in the 1960–70s; statistical HMM–GMM ASR in the 1990s; hybrid neural-HMM alternatives in the 2000s; RNN/LSTM deep-learning ASR around 2010; CTC and RNN-Transducer end-to-end ASR in the mid-2010s; attention, encoder-decoder, and Transformers at the source’s present. Treat eras as a simplified source timeline, not exact invention dates or a claim about the current state of the art. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside text.

ASR/STT maps acoustic speech to words or discrete text tokens. It is distinct from semantic interpretation and TTS. The waveform-to-text figure says “It’s time for lunch!” Modern systems may support language identification, translation, and speech-activity decisions, but multitask support does not imply every task is performed simultaneously on every call. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside text.

Microphone converts acoustic pressure into an analog electrical signal; the diagram orders speech, microphone/waveform, ASR, text, language understanding, and robot action. Digital Signal is labeled after ASR, but digital processing also requires sampling/quantization before model inference. The analog voltage exactly mimics the acoustic shape only as an idealization of a real microphone transfer function. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside text.

Waveform axes are amplitude versus time, with a short approximately periodic segment from 0 to 0.03875 seconds. Amplitude relates to loudness under otherwise comparable conditions; repetition frequency relates to pitch, not a universal single-frequency description of all speech. Speech begins as varying air pressure and must be digitized for the illustrated processing. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside text.

Feature pipeline figure: digitization, windowing/framing, DFT, log-Mel spectrum, then MFCC. Acronyms DFT and MFCC expanded. Output is a sequence of acoustic feature vectors. Whisper uses log-Mel input rather than requiring the final MFCC/DCT step; the entire pictured chain is not mandatory for every ASR model. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside text.

Digitization is sampling followed by quantization. Sampling gives discrete times at a rate such as 16 kHz; quantization maps measured amplitudes to finite levels, illustrated by 8- or 16-bit integers. Sampling alone does not quantize amplitude. Nyquist frequency is half the sampling rate; a bandlimited signal and boundary/phase conditions are needed for accurate reconstruction, not the unqualified at-least-twice slogan. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside text.

Speech is nonstationary but short frames are treated as approximately stationary. The three window parameters are size, stride, and shape. Multiplication y[n] = w[n]s[n] selects and weights samples; it is not convolution. Window length and stride are different, allowing overlap. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside text.

Rectangular and Hamming equations and both waveform plots inspected. The printed Hamming formula is 0.54 − 0.46 cos(2πn/L), 0 ≤ n ≤ L−1: a periodic convention, unlike symmetric denominator L−1. The claim that Hamming reaches zero at its boundaries is false: w[0] = 0.08. The prose calls L a number of frames although the formula indexes samples. Smooth curves illustrate already discrete sampled inputs. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside text.

DFT equation X[k] = Σ x[n] exp(−j2πkn/N), n from 0 to N−1, and waveform-to-spectrum figure inspected. DFT gives complex magnitude/phase coefficients; FFT is an efficient algorithm for the same transform. The source uses a 25 ms Hamming-windowed frame and a frequency axis to 8000 Hz. Magnitude/power and dB scaling are later representations rather than the raw complex DFT itself. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside text.

Overlapping triangular Mel filters are narrower and more closely spaced at low physical frequencies, wider at high frequencies. Their energy outputs form the Mel spectrum. The displayed convention is mel(f) = 1127 ln(1 + f/700), with f in Hz. This is one Mel convention, not all library defaults. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside text.

Each filter yields one scalar channel energy; the vector contains M channels. Logarithm is applied elementwise. The notation m_i refers ambiguously to filter and output energy; distinguish the weighted filter from its scalar response. Actual Whisper preprocessing also includes implementation-specific clamping, scaling, and feature-count conventions, so the generic log vector alone is not the exact numerical implementation. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside text.

MFCCs capture a compact spectral-envelope/vocal-tract representation. A cepstrum plot shows amplitude against sample index. Overall energy and dynamic features are named, but these depend on whether energy and temporal delta features are included; a single static MFCC vector does not automatically contain temporal derivatives. Whisper uses log-Mel features instead of requiring MFCCs. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside text.

Traditional ASR: acoustic HMM–GMM model, pronunciation lexicon mapping words to phonemes, language model, and search decoder. The claim that every component is independently trained is too broad: a lexicon may be curated and a decoder is a search algorithm. End-to-end networks can combine modeling roles, but do not eliminate all preprocessing, search, or optional language-model integration. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside text.

Sequence mismatch example: features every 10 ms, acoustic sequence 5 to 19 times text length. The ratio depends on tokenization, duration, and speech rate and is not universal. The Venn diagram places ASR at machine learning, signal processing, and NLP. Subsampling reduces length but alone does not solve variable speech/text alignment. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside text.

One-frame temporal CNN illustration: z_j = x_j w_0 for 1 ≤ j ≤ t, with local dot products. The stride-one same-length statement is true for this one-frame case or suitable padding, not arbitrary valid convolutions. The scalar equation suppresses vector/channel dimensions. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside text.

Odd-width kernel equation z_j = Σ from i=−p to p of x_(j+i) w_(i+p). Here p acts as half-width; equal zero padding can preserve length at stride one. Diagram shows padded edges and a three-weight kernel. A second equation sums channel convolutions but suppresses distinct per-channel weights and output channels. Stride greater than one reduces temporal length but need not skip every sample contribution or by itself solve alignment. Deep-learning Conv1d generally implements cross-correlation rather than weight-reversed mathematical convolution. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside text.

Encoder-decoder diagram: 80-dimensional log-Mel frames, subsampling into shorter sequence X, encoder contextual output H, decoder receiving a start symbol and shifted previous text to predict “it’s time…”. Encoder listens and decoder generates one character or subword token at a time. This is the architecture shown, not a requirement for all ASR systems. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside text.

Cross-attention uses Q from decoder hidden states and K,V from encoder acoustic representations. Equations Q=H_dec WQ, K=H_enc WK, V=H_enc WV and softmax(QKᵀ/√d_k)V inspected. Diagram includes encoder self-attention, decoder causal self-attention, decoder cross-attention, normalization, feedforward layers, residual paths, and a language-modeling output head. Cross-attention is standard in encoder-decoder Transformers, not a new addition unique to speech. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside text.

Causal decoder self-attention uses prior text, unlike acoustic cross-attention. Greedy decoding selects the highest conditional next-token probability and feeds that token back. The source uses characters as an illustration; modern tokenizers may use subwords. Local greedy choices do not guarantee the highest joint sequence probability. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside text.

Autoregressive product conditions every term on audio and earlier tokens, although the displayed left side omits the conditioning on X. Scoring is literally log P(Y|X)/|Y|_c + λ log P_LM(Y): only the acoustic term is length-normalized, not the whole sum. External LM influence is controlled by λ. This is an example scoring rule, not proof that default Whisper decoding uses external LM fusion. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside text.

Whisper diagram labels sinusoidal position encoding on the audio encoder and learned positional encoding on the text decoder. The prose incorrectly calls audio positions learned. The blanket 128-channel feature claim needs a model/version qualification: the following code names whisper-small. Two Conv1D+GELU stages precede the encoder, and cross-attention connects encoder to autoregressive decoder. Task/language/timestamp and start tokens are drawn; multilingual task support is not necessarily simultaneous output of every task. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside text.

Full 18-line Python raster snippet transcribed: transformers WhisperProcessor and WhisperForConditionalGeneration; torch and torchaudio; model openai/whisper-small; pretrained processor/model; torchaudio.load of /content/sample_audio.mp3; resampling to 16000 Hz when needed; audio.squeeze().numpy(); processor return_tensors=pt; torch.no_grad; model.generate(input_features); batch_decode(skip_special_tokens=True)[0]. Stereo squeeze does not downmix. Source audio and weights are external prerequisites; the printed dinner sentence is reported output, not a reproduction. The snippet has no print statement despite the displayed Transcription label. A linked complete notebook and embedded-looking audio icon require separate retrieval checks. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside text.

Applications: robot conversational command transcription, human-computer interfaces, media captions, and accessibility for difficulty typing or hearing. Text output is an input to interpretation, not sufficient semantic understanding or safe robot execution by itself. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside text.

Post-ASR pipeline: text transcription, language understanding/response generation, then text-to-speech. An LLM is the source’s example implementation, not the only possible NLU method. TTS reverses the input/output modality direction but is not a mathematical inverse recovering the original speaker/prosody. Speech-to-speech models may use discrete acoustic tokens to bypass an explicit text transcript. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside text.

Cleaner refers to working-fluid leakage, not a guarantee of zero exhaust contamination. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside text.

Brushed DC text: stationary brushes contact revolving commutator to energize rotor windings; torque proportional to winding current in the stated model; winding overheating limits sustained operation. Electric motors are controllable and easy to interface. The unlabelled cutaway is generic motor imagery and is not proof of a visible brushed commutator. Relative fluid-versus-electric power density depends on the comparison boundary. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside text.

Brushless: stationary windings and rotating magnetic rotor, electronic commutation from shaft position, reduced brush wear and favorable cooling. Internal shaft sensor is an example, not mandatory because sensorless commutation exists. Claims of infrequent AC motors and low-torque steppers need historical/task qualification, not current blanket truth. Better cooling and torque are design-dependent. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside text.

Five gripper boxes inspected: two-finger parallel for boxes/warehouse; three-finger adaptive for irregular shapes; vacuum for flat packages/glass; inflatable silicone soft fingers for delicate food/medical; magnetic for metal sheets/castings. Magnetic attraction needs suitable material, not all metals. Vacuum needs an appropriate seal/surface and payload margin. End-effector is terminal tool/device, not necessarily the structural last link itself. Simpler action space can ease learning but does not guarantee task success. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside text.

Current is a torque estimate via a motor model, not direct contact wrench. Tactile arrays give spatial contact distribution. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside text.
